title: Rival publics assign threat and alliance roles differently across the same global order
source_unit: Pew Research Center Spring 2026 Global Attitudes Survey; India, Pakistan, Bangladesh, and Sri Lanka comparative samples
geography: South Asia, with detailed India-Pakistan comparison

observations.period: India fieldwork February 8-April 27, 2026; Pakistan fieldwork April 8-May 7, 2026; report August 13, 2026

denominator.unit: Indian adults surveyed; separate samples include 1039 Pakistani, 1044 Bangladeshi, and 2513 Sri Lankan adults

bilateral_unfavorable_views.value: 78% of Indians view Pakistan unfavorably; roughly 90% of Pakistanis view India unfavorably, including 73% very unfavorable

greatest_threat.value: 54% of Indians name Pakistan as greatest threat; 43% of Pakistanis name India; 21% of Indians name China, while 24% of Pakistanis name Israel and 24% name the U.S. as next-greatest threats
greatest_threat.unit: percent naming country as greatest or next-greatest geopolitical threat

most_important_ally.value: 75% of Pakistanis name China as their most important ally; 36% of Indians name Russia and 16% name the U.S.
most_important_ally.unit: percent naming country as most important ally

within_india_difference.value: 34% of Indian Muslims versus 57% of Hindus name Pakistan as India's greatest threat; 21% of Indian Muslims versus 6% of Hindus view Pakistan favorably

observations.method: Face-to-face nationally designed surveys asking bilateral favorability, perceived threat, important ally, commitment to good relations, and views of major powers and leaders.
observations.uncertainty: The surveys are cross-sectional and field periods differed across countries. Threat and ally labels are perceptions, not measures of military capability, dependence, treaty reliability, or actual diplomatic behavior.
observations.subgroup: Adults in India, Pakistan, Bangladesh, and Sri Lanka; India results are also separated by religion, and the source reports country-specific views of the U.S., China, and Russia.
observations.counterinterpretation: Public threat judgments may reflect recent conflict, national identity, media environments, or survey timing rather than stable alliance preferences. Favorable views of a power do not establish policy alignment or material dependence.

boundary: This record adds a comparative geopolitical-public-opinion layer. It does not infer alliance behavior, strategic dependence, military balance, or causal effects from perceived threat and partner rankings.
